newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Euro shares forge higher on U.S. jobs report.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Euro shares forge higher on U.S. jobs report.

text.p: European shares mostly extended their earlier gains on Friday afternoon when the U.S. government's jobs report for April showed that the rise in employment was less than expected.

The U.S. Labor Department said 142,000 non-farm jobs were added to payrolls in April, little changed from a revised 139,000 that were created in March, and far fewer than the 211,000 rise which Wall Street economists had expected on average.
The fall took the U.S. unemployment rate to 4.9 percent -- its lowest rate in more than 23 years -- from 5.2 percent in March.

There is "very little evidence in these numbers of upward pressure on wages. They mean the Fed will put (interst rate) policy on hold for another two months to look at additional employment reports," one U.S economist said.

The U.S. Federal Reserve central bank plays close attention to jobs figures in gauging inflation pressures. It has nudged rates higher once already this year to counter inflation and meets again to review policy on May 20.
U.S. stocks were expected to receive a boost from the figures and the 30-year Treasury bond was up 6/32 to yield 6.90 percent shortly after the release of the data.
By 1300 gmt, London's FTSE was up 0.4 percent at 4,462.2, just below its 4,466.5 trading high which was set on April 30, while shares in Paris and Frankfurt were up 0.3 and 0.65 percent respectively.
In Paris, the CAC-40 index was 7.70 points higher at 2,647.16. In Frankfurt, the DAX index of leading shares was up 22.3 points at 3,455.62.
London shares were slightly higher at midday after digesting the Labour party's emphatic win in Britain's general election and recouping early modest losses.
The huge election rout for Britain's Conservative party, which had held power for 18 years, put Labour in government with a majority of about 180 seats.
For many of the FTSE's large exporting companies whose earnings have been squeezed by the sterling's strength in recent months a weakness in the pound was a boon.

"There's an argument that we've known Labour was going to get in for months," said a dealer at a major securities house, "and now they've got such a huge majority there's a degree of certainty so we could see the market go higher."

"The big questions now are on the econonmy and taxation, policy towards Europe and the constitution," another dealer said. "There are some real minefields for them to negotiate and we shall have to wait and see what they do."

One of Labour's first tests comes with next week's planned monetary policy meeting, at which the Bank of England is expected to repeat its call for higher interest rates. Next month Labour is expected to deliver its first budget.
"Labour has inherited an economy in good shape," a dealer said. "The question is whether they can keep it that way."
British gilts fell in early trade but had rallied by midday when the long gilt future was up 7/32 at 111.0 having been as low as 110-05/32.
Sterling, too, had hauled itself off its earlier lows by early afternoon when it stood at around 1.6115 to the dollar having been as low as 1.6008, compared with 1.6253 late on Thursday.

Sterling firmed against the dollar and mark overnight, but came under pressure in early trade when dealers cited a column in the Times newspaper which said Britain's new government "must create conditions for an immediate fall in the pound" to avoid economic damage.
The dollar drifted higher against the mark and yen at Europe's midday ahead of the U.S. data after which it shed some of its gains.
STOCKS PRICES AT 1300 GMT
London's FTSE 100 was up 17.2 points at 4,462.2.
The Paris CAC-40 index was up 7.7 points at 2,647.16.
Frankfurt's DAX index was up 22.3 points at 3,460.37.
CURRENCIES AT 1300 GMT
The dollar stood at 1.7230 marks compared with 1.7182 marks late in Europe on Thursday. It wasen after 126.57 yen late on Thursday.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold fixed at $339.80 an ounce in the morning compared with Thursday's close of $340.80 in London.
